messages.subject: Rolling (staggered) camera deployment in single-season occupancy — how to identify seasonal detection effects?
messages.subject_clean: Rolling (staggered) camera deployment in single-season occupancy — how to identify seasonal detection effects?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to analyse camera trap data for garden dormice (Eliomys quercinus) in Germany, using single-season occupancy model, and I would be grateful for advice on a design problem.

The sampling was initially just done for presence/absence data and not with a later analysis in mind. As a result of that, and due to a limited amount of cameras, cameras were not deployed simultaneously. They were moved around in a rolling fashion over the season, which gives the following structure:
79 sites, 22 weekly occasions (May to October 2025)
523 of 1,738 site-occasions actually sampled (30 %); mean 6.6 occasions per site
start dates spread over a 134-day window
between 11 and 26 cameras running at any one time
52 detections at 24 sites

Missing occasions appear unrelated to site quality and sites with and without detections ran for a median of 31 and 33 days respectively. So I believe the missingness is at random with respect to occupancy state.

My difficulty is with the detection sub-model. Because each site covers only a short window of the season, calendar time and site identity are almost completely confounded. A month-as-factor model for p performs worst in my candidate set and models using julian-date do not do much better. Models using temperature work to some extent but the we have a similar problem here. Temperature varies both within sites (across the season) and between them (elevation, aspect), and because each site covers a different window, its mean temperature is itself confounded with the deployment period.

Has anyone worked with data from this kind of rolling deployment before? I would be grateful for any suggestions on how to deal with it, or for pointers to studies that faced something similar.

And more generally: with calendar time unidentifiable, is it defensible to model p with covariates that have no seasonal interpretation at all (effort, bait age, weather) and simply state that seasonal variation in detectability could not be estimated? Or does that understate the problem?

Many thanks,
Jakob

messages.subject: Random vs preferential camera placement within sites: does it bias occupancy?
messages.subject_clean: Random vs preferential camera placement within sites: does it bias occupancy?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to ask your opinion on a study design question that is generating some discussion in our team.

We run a camera trap project for medium and large mammals (wolf, lynx and several mesocarnivores). Sites are selected at random, and each camera is placed near the random point, within a buffer, in a spot where it can work properly (good field of view, no continuous false triggers). After two years, detection probability is very low for some species, and in some cases we cannot even fit null models.

The proposal is to add a second camera at each site: one camera stays at the random point, and the other is placed on the best spot nearby (e.g. a trail or forest road) within the buffer, following a rule defined in advance and applied in the same way at all sites. The placement type would be recorded and used as a covariate in the detection submodel, and the two cameras would be kept as separate replicates of the same site.

The argument in favour is that, if the site is the area around the random point, moving a camera inside the site to a trail changes detection but not occupancy, and this is exactly what the detection submodel is for. The argument against is that we are oversampling features that the species prefer, which could bias the estimates, especially if occupancy is interpreted closer to the point level.

My questions are:
1. Do you think this within-site preferential placement can bias occupancy estimates, as long as sites are random and placement type is modelled in detection?
2. Since all our species have home ranges much larger than the camera field of view, and home range size varies a lot among them, how would you define the buffer (the site) in a meaningful way?
3. Would a multi-scale occupancy model (site occupancy, local use at the camera, detection) be a better framework here?
4. Any other risks we should consider, for example if trails and roads are correlated with the habitat covariates we use for occupancy?

Any thoughts, experiences or references would be very welcome.
Thanks a lot,

Simone

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Random vs preferential camera placement within sites: does it bias occupancy?
messages.body_plain:
My two cents - you can think about this in terms of bias, or you can think about it in terms of whether and how available inference from your occupancy estimates change under different designs. I think putting the camera traps along trails as you describe it sounds similar to timing breeding bird surveys during peak singing in the morning. The catch is that you need to keep in mind if and how the overlap between the sampled area and space use / territories might change under alternative designs. I'd have to think about your other questions more to offer useful responses. Instead, I'll offer a couple papers that might help you (and maybe your team) think through your questions.

Quresh S. Latif
Biometrician
Bird Conservancy of the Rockies
230 Cherry St., Ste. 150, Fort Collins, CO 80521
970-482-1707 (ext. 15)
Connecting people, birds and land
www.birdconservancy.org <http://www.birdconservancy.org/>
